lesson.subject: literacy
lesson.title: Malala's Voice
lesson.subtitle: Term 4 Week 6, Session 3
lesson.footer: Persuasive Speeches | Year 5/6 Literacy | Week 6 Session 3

plan.curriculum: English 2.0, Level 5: VC2E5LY09 evaluating ideas in a spoken text; VC2E5LY07 how a text reflects the time and place it was created; VC2E5LY10 creating spoken texts with elaborated ideas
plan.shape: listen, map, story, list: Malala's UN speech is mapped on the listening grid, then students practise a true small story that proves a point and a list that builds
plan.criticalFeature: a true small story makes a big idea feel real, and a list that builds carries the audience to the big point
decisionPoints: the choice check: the story that proves the point
the exit board: a short story for a new claim
plan.anchor: Claim it. Prove it. Sell it. Say it. Today: a true story sells it.
plan.catchUp: Missed earlier sessions? Show the listening grid; it is the same for every speaker. The story frame needs nothing from before.

routineIcons: Write it, chin it, show me
Point to A, B or C
boardSetup: Listening grid: Message? Audience? Think? Feel? Do?
Story frame: Then... One day... Now... So...
videos: DCE Speech Collection: Malala Yousafzai, UN speech, 2013 (teacher's copy; play the opening and the 'one child, one teacher' section)

resources.label: Worksheet
resources.description: Your turn: map Malala's speech, judge stories, build lists, then tell your own true story for your issue.
resources.title: Malala's Voice
resources.subtitle: A true story makes a big idea real.

example.prompt: Any speech: message, audience, think, feel, do.
example.answer: Message: every child deserves to go to school.

items.prompt: Fill in the listening grid for Malala's speech.
rows: What she wants them to think
What she wants them to feel
What she wants them to do
answers: Her message in one sentence
Every child, especially every girl, deserves an education.
Her audience
young people and leaders at the United Nations
What she wants them to think
education is the answer
What she wants them to feel
hope, courage, determination
What she wants them to do
speak up and support education for all

example.prompt: Claim: we need a crossing guard.
steps: Tell it in two or three sentences
example.answer: Last week a car missed my little brother by a metre. That's why we need a crossing guard.

items.prompt: Claim: our school needs a buddy bench. Which story proves it?
options: In Prep, I sat alone every lunch until someone noticed.
items.explain: A real moment of loneliness that a buddy bench would fix.

items.prompt: Zara told this story in her speech. Find the problem and fix it.
work: Last summer we went to the beach and it was fun and we had ice cream.
items.answer: It doesn't prove any point. Fix: Last summer I found a turtle tangled in plastic. That's why bags must go.

example.prompt: Claim: one person can make a difference.
example.answer: One bottle. One bin. One school. One planet.

items.prompt: Write a list that builds for each claim.
answers: Small actions add up.
One light. One tap. One trip. One planet.
Kids can lead change.
One voice, one class, one school, one world.
Every tree matters.
Shade for one child, home for one bird, air for us all.

steps: So: link it to your claim
example.answer: Last year I saw a bear at a zoo. It paced the same path, over and over. That's when I knew.

items.prompt: Write a short true story (3-5 sentences) for your speech that makes your issue feel real. End with: That's why...
items.answer: A small true moment, told simply, linked to the claim.

resources.tip: Finished? Add Malala to your Toolkit, then grab the Extension.

resources.label: Extension
resources.description: Early finisher option: make a story specific, then write one for a different audience.
resources.title: Story Crafter
resources.subtitle: The best speech stories are small, true and specific.

example.prompt: Vague: Once I saw some rubbish.
steps: Add a detail you could see or hear
example.answer: Last Tuesday, a chip packet was stuck in the creek grate. A duck was pecking at it. I felt sick.

items.prompt: Rewrite each vague story with specific details.
rows: One time I was hot at school.
I saw an animal that was sad.
Something bad happened at the beach.
answers: One time I was hot at school.
Last February, our classroom hit 34 degrees and Ella fainted.
I saw an animal that was sad.
At the show, a pony stood in the sun with no water.
Something bad happened at the beach.
At Easter, I pulled a fishing line off a seagull's leg.

example.prompt: Story for my class vs story for the council.
steps: What does this audience care about?
example.answer: For the council: the same story, plus how many students it affects.

items.prompt: Retell your true story for a different audience. Explain one thing you changed and why.
items.answer: A retold story with a change linked to the new audience.

resources.label: Supported Worksheet
resources.description: Supported option: picture-clue choices, a first story line done and a frame.
resources.title: Malala Helper
resources.subtitle: Then, one day, now, so.

items.prompt: What does Malala want every child to have?
items.hint: Think about one book and one pen.

items.prompt: How does she want us to feel?

example.prompt: 'Last week I tripped on the broken path.'

rows: Last week I tripped on the broken path.
Yesterday my bag got soaked in the rain.
answers: Last week I tripped on the broken path.
story
Paths should be safe.
statement
Yesterday my bag got soaked in the rain.
story
items.hint: The first one is done for you.

example.answer: Last year, I visited a zoo. I saw a bear pacing. That's why bears need space.

items.prompt: Finish: Last ___, I ___. I saw ___. That's why ___.
items.answer: A short true story linked to the issue.
items.hint: Think of something you really saw or did.

slides.notes: Open the session. One line: today we hear from a girl who spoke up for every child's right to go to school.

Cue the selected section of Malala Yousafzai's 2013 UN speech from the DCE Speech Collection. Print the Worksheet for everyone, the Extension for early finishers and the Supported Worksheet for those who need it. Toolkits out.

slides.learningIntention: We are learning how a true story and a building list make a speech powerful.
successCriteria: I can say a speaker's message and audience.
I can tell a short true story that proves my point.
I can write a list that builds to a big idea.

beats: POINT to the learning intention.
SAY: Today we learn how one true story can move the whole world.
SAY: Read the I can lines with me. Everyone, together, on three.
SAY: The first one is where we all start.
The second one is today's main goal.
notes.prep: SC1 is reachable for all; SC2 is the core and the exit evidence; SC3 is the stretch.

slides.title: Imagine school was taken away
lines: Imagine being told: girls can't go to school any more.
Would you speak up, even if it was risky?

notes.answer: open - most would want to; some would be scared
beats: SAY: In parts of Pakistan, girls were told they could not go to school.
One girl, Malala, spoke up anyway.
ASK: Would you speak up, even if it was risky?
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: a mix
ASK: What would you say to make the world listen?
20 sec. Turn and tell, partner A first.
EXPECT: school matters; it's not fair; everyone deserves to learn
SAY: Malala was attacked for speaking up. She survived.
At 16, she spoke at the United Nations.
trap: focusing on the attack rather than her message.
Fix: say the attack is why her story is
powerful; the message is about school for every child.
notes.care: Keep details of the 2012 attack brief and calm; check in quietly with anyone upset.
notes.prep: SOURCES: Malala Yousafzai, UN Youth Assembly, New York, 12 July 2013 (her 16th birthday).

slides.meaning: A short true story that makes a point.
slides.example: I sat alone every lunch in Prep. That's why we need a buddy bench.

notes.answer: a short true story that makes a point
beats: POINT to the word. SAY: Anecdote. Say it with me. Anecdote.
SAY: A short true story that makes a point.
ASK: Tell your partner a ten-second true story about lunchtime.
10 sec. Turn and tell, partner B first.
EXPECT: a real moment, short, with a point
trap: thinking any story is an anecdote, even a made-up one.
Fix: say a speech anecdote must be true, or the audience stops trusting you.

rows: young people and leaders at the UN
speak up; support school for all

beats: PLAY the selected section from the DCE Speech Collection.
SAY: Listen for her own story, and for a list that builds.
POINT to Message.
SAY: Her story is about her, but her message is about every child.
POINT to Feel.
SAY: She doesn't make us feel sorry for her.
She makes us feel hopeful. That's a choice.
ASK: What does she want the audience to do?
10 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: speak up; support education
trap: writing her story as her message.
Fix: ask what does she want for every child? That's the message.
notes.prep: The model: the same listening grid as Session 2. CARE: some students may find the attack upsetting; keep the focus on her message.

visual.text: "One child, one teacher, one book and one pen can change the world."

notes.answer: repeated one, building from a child to the world
beats: READ it aloud, slowly, with a pause after each one.
SAY: Four small things. Then the biggest thing of all: the world.
POINT to each one.
SAY: Repeating one makes each thing feel small and possible. Anyone can do one.
ASK: Say it with me, pausing after each one.
3 sec. Cue: Everyone, together, on three.
EXPECT: the line, with pauses
ASK: Why end with change the world?
15 sec. Turn and tell, partner B first.
EXPECT: it's the biggest idea; it lands last
trap: Fix: student orders from smallest to biggest.
notes.stretch: Write a list that builds for your own issue.
notes.help: Use her pattern: One ___, one ___, one ___ can ___.
notes.prep: SOURCES: check the wording against your DCE copy. Toolkit row 4.

slides.title: Story or statement?
slides.pivot: ask: did something happen to someone?
slides.followUp: cold call one student: what point could that story prove?

items.text: Last winter, the oval flooded and our grand final was cancelled.
My nan grew up with no library, so she read the same book forty times.

say: One finger statement. Two fingers story.
trap: calling any sentence with I in it a story.
Fix: ask did something actually happen? Student re-votes.
notes.stretch: Say which claim each story could prove.
notes.help: Look for a time: last winter, yesterday.

slides.title: Which story proves the point?
slides.prompt: Claim: kids should learn first aid at school.

options.text: I once watched a movie about doctors.
options.misconception: a story, but it doesn't prove the point

options.text: When my brother choked, my friend knew what to do.
First aid is very important for everyone.

notes.answer: B - a real moment where first aid mattered
beats: SAY: Three lines for a speech on first aid. Which one proves it?
ASK: Which story proves the point?
10 sec. Cue: voices off, everyone points to A, B or C.
EXPECT: pointing to B
SCAN the room, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, cold call: what feeling does B give the audience?
Less -> ask does it show the claim is true? for each, re-ask.
REVEAL after pointing is scanned.
SAY: B. A real moment. You can feel why first aid matters.
trap: pointing to C because it sounds sure.
Fix: ask did anything happen in C? Student re-chooses.
notes.prep: Decision point before writing. Under 80% means the class builds one story together with the frame.

slides.title: Build the list
slides.pivot: repeat one starting word, then order small to big
slides.followUp: cold call one board: perform it with pauses

items.answer: One bottle. One bin. One habit. One planet.
items.expect: a repeated word, small to big

items.answer: One book, one reader, one idea can change a life.

items.text: Claim: our class can lead the school.
items.answer: One class. One voice. One whole school following.

say: Write a list that builds, Malala style.
trap: a list that doesn't build: one cat, one dog, one fish.
Fix: ask what is the biggest? Put it last.
notes.stretch: Make your list a rule of three instead of four.

slides.title: Tell a true story
slides.task: Work through your Worksheet. Finish with a short true story for your speech that makes your issue feel real. Add Malala to your Toolkit.

notes.answer: a short true story ending in That's why...
beats: POINT to the task.
SAY: A small, true moment beats a big claim. What have you seen or done?
SAY: Read the task, complete each part, check your work.
Finished? Extension next. Everyone, together, on three.
CIRCULATE. Ask: is it true? What's the point it proves?
ASK: Tell your story to your partner in under 30 seconds.
30 sec each. Turn and tell, partner A first.
EXPECT: a real moment linked to a claim
trap: a long story with no point.
Fix: student finishes with That's why... and cuts anything before it that doesn't matter.
notes.stretch: Extension: make a story specific, then retell it for a new audience.
notes.help: Supported Worksheet: picture-clue choices, a first line done, a story frame.
notes.prep: Independent application. Toolkit rows 3 and 4 filled before the exit. SC2 and SC3.

slides.extendedTask: a worksheet ending in a short true story for the student's speech

slides.title: Show what you know
questions: Claim: every school should teach swimming.
Write a two-sentence true-sounding story that proves it.

notes.answer: e.g. My cousin slipped into the river. She could swim, so she was safe.
beats: SAY: A new claim. Prove it with a short story.
ASK: Write a two-sentence story that proves the claim.
60 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: something happened, linked to swimming
RECORD who writes a statement instead of a story. Tomorrow's warm-up.
trap: Fix: none now, record the name.
notes.prep: Exit evidence for SC2 on a new claim. One board per student.

slides.reflectionPrompt: Which is stronger in a speech: a fact or a story? Tell your partner why.

notes.answer: open - a story, because people feel it; a fact, because it's proof
beats: SAY: Let's read our I can lines together. Everyone, together, on three.
ASK: How sure are you that you can tell a story that proves your point?
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: thumbs up, sideways or down
RECORD each thumb down beside the exit boards.
ASK: Which is stronger in a speech:
a fact or a story? Tell your partner why.
20 sec. Turn and tell, partner B first.
EXPECT: a story, because people feel it; a fact, because it's proof
notes.prep: Self-assessment read beside the exit boards. Toolkit rows 3-4 filled. SC2.
